## The same component, in two languages {visibility="uncounted"}

| | `primarycensored`, R and Stan | `CensoredDistributions.jl` |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a distribution | New branch, new integer, rebuild | Pass the type |
| Distributions covered | 18, listed in a switch | Any univariate one |
| Choosing one | An integer, set before sampling | The object itself |
| Sharing the code | Copy 1,081 lines of Stan in | A line in `Project.toml` |
| The integral | `integrate_1d`, then an ODE recast | 64 fixed nodes |
| Worst failure | 243 of 256 chains died | Broken on 3 of 6 backends |

::: {.callout-important}
The Stan file has to know every distribution it will ever support. The
Julia file does not have to know any of them.
:::

## What the move fixed, and what it did not {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Removed**

A class of bug. `dist_id = 3` meant Normal in Stan and Weibull in R, so
asking for a Weibull fitted a normal and returned numbers. Every
distribution was affected except lognormal, gamma and exponential.

`primary_censored(Weibull(2, 1), Uniform(0, 1))` carries the type. There
is no second table for it to disagree with.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Moved**

The numerical problem, from the language to the autodiff backends. 82 of
929 issues and pull requests are about autodiff or numerics.

The default solver is `GaussLegendre(; n = 64)` because fixed nodes
trace through every backend and adaptive ones do not. Stan gave up
adaptive quadrature for an ODE. Julia gave it up for a dot product.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Unchanged**

Who uses it. 11,211 downloads all time against 116, and 511 last month
against 49.

Every package that depends on either one is mine, Sam Brand's or
Sebastian Funk's. The two packages are a month apart in age, so some of
that gap is R having the users and some is the package.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-important}
The composition is the reusable part. The package is only where the
censoring happens to live.
:::
